cases.title: A fast rhythm, then a change
cases.stem: A 64-year-old has a regular broad-complex tachycardia at 190/min, BP 72/40, confusion and a palpable pulse. The team is at the bedside.

steps.prompt: Which immediate plan best matches these findings?

options.text: Prepare urgent synchronized cardioversion with the resuscitation team.
options.why: Poor perfusion with this regular tachycardia and a pulse calls for urgent synchronized treatment.

options.text: Wait for a formal cardiology report.
options.why: The patient is unstable; waiting delays time-critical care.

options.text: Use the pulse rate alone to decide on discharge.
options.why: Rate does not establish stability; hypotension and confusion are major concerns.

steps.update: The team prepares cardioversion. Before it is delivered, the patient becomes unresponsive; no definite pulse is found promptly, and the monitor shows ventricular fibrillation.

options.text: Start the shockable cardiac-arrest pathway: CPR and unsynchronized defibrillation.
options.why: The patient now has a different clinical state. VF arrest requires defibrillation and CPR.

options.text: Continue trying to synchronize to the fibrillatory rhythm.
options.why: Synchronization is inappropriate for ventricular fibrillation.

options.text: Obtain a 12-lead ECG before starting CPR.
options.why: Diagnostic recording must not postpone resuscitation.

steps.update: Following resuscitation, a pulse returns. BP remains low and the patient is not following commands.
steps.prompt: What is the appropriate next destination?

options.text: Monitored post-arrest care with stabilization and investigation of the cause.
options.why: Return of a pulse does not end the need for critical care.

options.text: Discharge after the monitor shows sinus rhythm.
options.why: A normal rhythm does not establish recovery.

options.text: Remove monitoring to avoid alarms.
options.why: Ongoing instability requires monitoring and reassessment.

debrief: What observation changed the treatment pathway?
Explain the difference between treating a rhythm with a pulse and treating cardiac arrest.
Hand over the arrest rhythm, interventions, response and remaining instability.

cases.title: Deterioration after chest trauma
cases.stem: A 31-year-old arrives after blunt chest trauma. During initial assessment, BP falls to 78/46, respiratory distress worsens and breath sounds are markedly reduced on the left.

options.text: Assess and treat immediate thoracic threats during resuscitation.
options.why: This combination warrants urgent assessment for tension pneumothorax and other life threats.

options.text: Finish a routine history before reassessment.
options.why: The new deterioration changes the priority.

options.text: Assume anxiety explains the respiratory distress.
options.why: Shock and asymmetric examination need an urgent physical explanation.

steps.update: The treating team finds a compelling clinical picture of tension pneumothorax with severe compromise. CT is available on another floor.

options.text: Arrange immediate decompression by a trained clinician without waiting for CT.
options.why: Severe compromise with suspected tension physiology requires treatment before imaging.

options.text: Transfer to CT before treatment in every case.
options.why: Transfer would delay care in this unstable patient.

options.text: Wait for tracheal deviation to appear.
options.why: An absent late sign does not make the patient stable.

steps.update: After decompression, breathing improves but hypotension persists.
steps.prompt: What is the next reasoning step?

options.text: Repeat the primary survey and look for additional causes of shock.
options.why: An initial improvement does not explain persistent shock or exclude other injuries.

options.text: Stop investigating because one problem was treated.
options.why: Trauma can cause more than one life-threatening injury.

options.text: Use the improved breath sounds alone to discharge.
options.why: Persistent hypotension is incompatible with that conclusion.

debrief: Which findings supported treatment before imaging?
What other injuries could explain persistent shock?
Assign roles for reassessment, communication and definitive trauma care.

cases.title: An infant who becomes quieter
cases.stem: A 7-week-old with coryza has worsening work of breathing and is taking less than half the usual feeds. A parent reports a pause in breathing at home.

steps.prompt: Which feature most strongly supports urgent escalation?

options.text: The reported apnea, alongside the current respiratory difficulty.
options.why: A breathing pause in this infant warrants urgent assessment.

options.text: The presence of coryza alone.
options.why: Coryza is common and does not capture the immediate concern.

options.text: The family having no thermometer.
options.why: Equipment at home does not determine the severity of illness.

steps.update: While monitored, the infant develops a further apneic episode and becomes less responsive.

options.text: Call pediatric resuscitation support and support airway and breathing.
options.why: Apnea with reduced responsiveness requires immediate support.

options.text: Wait to see whether the next feed is easier.
options.why: Feeding is not the priority during apnea.

options.text: Assume reduced noise means improvement.
options.why: Becoming quieter can reflect exhaustion or deterioration.

steps.update: The infant improves with the team’s support but remains unable to feed adequately.
steps.prompt: Which disposition best fits the course?

options.text: Hospital care with ongoing respiratory and hydration assessment.
options.why: Apnea and inadequate feeding require continued assessment and support.

options.text: Discharge solely because one saturation reading improved.
options.why: A single number does not account for the apnea and feeding problem.

options.text: Offer a routine appointment several weeks later.
options.why: The immediate problems have not resolved.

debrief: How can a child appear quieter while becoming sicker?
What would you include in the parent’s explanation?
Discuss how age and comorbidity affect local thresholds.

cases.title: Pain and collapse in early pregnancy
cases.stem: A 28-year-old with a positive pregnancy test has lower abdominal pain, vaginal spotting and a fainting episode. BP is 84/48 and pulse is 124/min.

steps.prompt: What is the safest initial approach?

options.text: Resuscitate and obtain urgent obstetric/gynecologic assessment for possible internal bleeding.
options.why: Instability in early pregnancy needs emergency assessment; ectopic pregnancy is a concern.

options.text: Book routine outpatient follow-up as the only plan.
options.why: That does not address current shock.

options.text: Assume light external bleeding excludes major hemorrhage.
options.why: External bleeding does not quantify internal blood loss.

steps.update: The team starts resuscitation. No intrauterine pregnancy has yet been confirmed; a laboratory result is pending.

options.text: Urgent specialist assessment and management of the unstable patient.
options.why: Pending tests must not defer the response to hemodynamic instability.

options.text: Wait for a single hormone result before seeking help.
options.why: One laboratory value cannot make this clinical state safe.

options.text: Require the patient to walk to another clinic.
options.why: An unstable patient needs supported care and appropriate transfer.

steps.update: BP improves transiently, but pain and tachycardia continue.
steps.prompt: How should that response affect disposition?

options.text: Continue emergency assessment and definitive planning with the specialist team.
options.why: A temporary response does not establish resolution of the cause.

options.text: Discharge because the last BP was better.
options.why: A transient improvement is not sufficient.

options.text: Stop observations to reduce anxiety.
options.why: The unresolved presentation needs continued reassessment.

debrief: Why can visible bleeding underestimate the problem?
What information belongs in the urgent referral?
How would you explain uncertainty while resuscitation continues?

cases.title: Awake, then drowsy again
cases.stem: A 40-year-old is found drowsy with very slow breathing and a palpable pulse. Opioid exposure is suspected; the amount and timing are unknown.

steps.prompt: Which priority best addresses the immediate threat?

options.text: Support breathing and give an opioid antagonist according to the local pathway.
options.why: Respiratory depression is the immediate concern; antidote treatment accompanies support.

options.text: Wait for a toxicology screen before helping ventilation.
options.why: Testing must not delay breathing support.

options.text: Focus only on making the person fully alert.
options.why: Adequate ventilation is the critical physiological goal.

steps.update: After treatment, breathing improves. Later the respiratory rate falls again and the patient becomes difficult to wake.

options.text: Reassess and support ventilation; obtain further treatment and toxicology advice.
options.why: Recurrent respiratory depression can outlast an initial antagonist response.

options.text: Assume the first response guarantees recovery.
options.why: The new respiratory findings contradict that assumption.

options.text: Leave the patient unmonitored because the cause is known.
options.why: Knowing a likely cause does not remove the need for monitoring.

steps.update: Repeated support has been required; the substance may be long acting.
steps.prompt: What is the appropriate disposition principle?

options.text: Continue monitored care and tailor observation/treatment with expert advice.
options.why: Recurrence and uncertain exposure make a fixed brief observation rule unsuitable.

options.text: Use a universal short discharge time for every opioid.
options.why: Duration and recurrence vary with the exposure and clinical course.

options.text: Base discharge only on pupil size.
options.why: Pupil size is not an adequate assessment of recovery.

debrief: What endpoint matters more than wakefulness alone?
How do recurrent symptoms change your plan?
Include harm-reduction and follow-up needs after acute stabilization.

cases.title: A reassuring score is not the whole story
cases.stem: A 22-year-old presents after self-harm. Physical care is underway. The person is distressed and says they do not feel safe returning home.

steps.prompt: What should the team arrange alongside physical care?

options.text: A compassionate assessment of immediate safety and psychosocial needs.
options.why: The person’s concerns and needs require direct assessment.

options.text: Dismiss the concern because observations are normal.
options.why: Normal physical observations do not resolve psychological safety.

options.text: Delay all conversation until physical care has ended.
options.why: Support and assessment can occur alongside physical treatment.

steps.update: A checklist score is described as low, but the person still reports feeling unsafe and has little support.
steps.prompt: How should the score be used?

options.text: It must not determine discharge; assess the individual situation and safety needs.
options.why: Risk categories cannot substitute for a psychosocial assessment.

options.text: Use the low score as an automatic discharge rule.
options.why: This ignores the person’s reported concerns and circumstances.

options.text: Use the score to guarantee there will be no further self-harm.
options.why: Such tools cannot provide that guarantee.

steps.update: The team is developing a care plan with the person.
steps.prompt: What is an important part of planning any transition?

options.text: Agree support, follow-up and a collaborative safety plan with the appropriate team.
options.why: A transition needs a practical plan addressing identified needs.

options.text: Give generic reassurance without checking the plan is workable.
options.why: A plan must fit the person’s circumstances.

options.text: Assume agreement means every concern has disappeared.
options.why: Agreement does not replace checking understanding and remaining concerns.

debrief: What might a numeric score conceal?
How can you explore immediate safety without judgment?
Discuss capacity, safeguarding and local legal requirements with the supervising team.

modules.title: Procedural sedation preparation
modules.intro: Rehearse the preparation and recovery discussion with your supervisor.
sections: Before
Clarify the procedure, alternatives, consent and patient-specific risks.
Assign a qualified person to monitor the patient continuously, in addition to the procedural clinician.
Check oxygen, suction, airway rescue equipment, monitoring and the recovery plan.
During
Monitor ventilation as well as oxygenation; capnography can identify respiratory depression earlier.
Agree who pauses the procedure and manages a complication.
After
Reassess airway, breathing, circulation and recovery before transition.
Explain aftercare, supervision and return advice using the local discharge criteria.
modules.question: Who will monitor the patient while the procedure is performed?
modules.answer: A designated qualified team member with continuous monitoring responsibility, separate from the clinician performing the procedure.

modules.title: Cardioversion team preparation
modules.intro: A preparation exercise for a supervised team; use the actual device and local protocol in training.
sections: Prepare
Confirm rhythm, pulse and evidence of instability.
Identify team roles, pads, monitoring and airway support; consider sedation where feasible without delaying urgent treatment.
Verify
For synchronized cardioversion, verify synchronization markers on the actual device.
If the rhythm or pulse changes, reassess the pathway rather than continuing the original plan.
Reassess
Check rhythm, pulse and perfusion after treatment.
Anticipate recurrence and communicate the cause and next plan.
modules.question: What change would make the original synchronized plan inappropriate?
modules.answer: Cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation requires the shockable-arrest pathway and unsynchronized defibrillation.

modules.title: Chest emergency preparation
modules.intro: Prepare the team and equipment; technical insertion steps require supervised practical training.
sections: Recognize
Assess respiratory and circulatory compromise in the context of chest injury.
Escalate suspected tension physiology urgently when severely compromised.
Prepare
Identify the trained operator and local decompression equipment.
Allocate monitoring, analgesia support and definitive drainage roles.
Reassess
Repeat the primary survey after intervention.
Continue assessment for hemorrhage and additional injuries if shock persists.
modules.question: Does improved breathing after an intervention explain persistent hypotension?
modules.answer: No. Repeat the primary survey and investigate additional causes while continuing resuscitation.

modules.title: A focused SBAR handover
modules.intro: Practice aloud using a fictional case. No patient-identifiable information is needed.
sections: Situation
State who you are, who you are calling about and what requires attention now.
Background and assessment
Give relevant context, the current findings and the trend.
Explain your concern and what remains uncertain.
Recommendation
Make a clear request and agree who will do what, and when.
Check that the receiver understood the action and contingency plan.
modules.question: A colleague says “Please review when free” about an unstable patient. What would you improve?
modules.answer: State the instability, request immediate bedside review and agree the immediate actions and escalation plan.

modules.title: Leading a resuscitation huddle
modules.intro: Use this short simulation to practice shared priorities and explicit roles.
sections: Brief
Summarize the current problem and immediate priorities.
Assign roles by name and identify the next reassessment point.
Respond
Invite concerns when the patient or workload changes.
State decisions clearly and confirm that tasks have an owner.
Debrief
Ask what worked and what made care difficult.
Agree one specific improvement, an owner and a follow-up point.
modules.question: Two clinicians assume the other has called for help. What team habit could prevent this?
modules.answer: Assign the task to a named person and confirm completion; make the next escalation step explicit.

modules.title: Teach and review a difficult decision
modules.intro: For residents, fellows and specialists: turn a case discussion into a practical learning point.
sections: Elicit reasoning
Ask the learner for their leading explanation and strongest alternative.
Ask what finding would change their plan.
Explore uncertainty
Separate what was known at the time from what became clear later.
Identify a source or local policy that would help resolve the uncertainty.
Improve
Give one specific observation and a next practice task.
For a recurring system problem, choose a measurable improvement and revisit it.
modules.question: How can a debrief avoid hindsight bias?
modules.answer: Reconstruct the information available at the decision point before discussing the eventual outcome.
